meta.title: Rāmāyaṇa & Mahābhārata — a cited, multi-track timeline
meta.description: Textual history, in-story chronology, reception, traditional dating, and proofs — with scholarship and tradition kept distinct. Nothing here is presented as settled fact.
meta.note: Seed data. Contributions welcome — every node must carry a source; see data/SCHEMA.md.

nodes.title: Oral bardic origins
nodes.summary: Most scholars hold the Mahābhārata grew from an oral sūta (bardic) tradition before being written, expanding over centuries from a shorter core to its received ~100,000-verse length.

date.note: The window in which most scholars place the epic's compilation and growth.

sources.cite: Brockington, John (1998), The Sanskrit Epics. Leiden: Brill.
Hiltebeitel, Alf (2001), Rethinking the Mahābhārata. Univ. of Chicago Press.

nodes.title: Bhandarkar (Poona) critical edition
nodes.summary: Between 1919 and 1966 the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune collated hundreds of manuscripts to reconstruct the oldest recoverable common text of the Mahābhārata.

date.note: Publication span of the BORI critical edition, general editors V. S. Sukthankar then S. K. Belvalkar.

sources.cite: Sukthankar, V. S. et al. (eds.), The Mahābhārata (BORI critical edition, 1933–1966).

proof.what: A reconstructed archetype collated from roughly 1,259 manuscripts.
proof.establishes: The oldest recoverable common written text of the epic.
proof.doesNotEstablish: That the narrated events happened, nor a single 'original' authored text or its absolute date.

nodes.title: Composition of Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: The core of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa is generally dated by scholars to roughly the mid-first-millennium BCE, with Books 1 (Bāla) and 7 (Uttara) widely regarded as later additions to an original five-book core.

date.note: Datings vary; Books II–VI are usually held older than the framing Books I & VII.

sources.cite: Goldman, Robert P. (gen. ed.), The Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki, 7 vols. Princeton Univ. Press, 1984–2017.
Brockington, John (1998), The Sanskrit Epics. Leiden: Brill.

nodes.title: Baroda critical edition of the Rāmāyaṇa
nodes.summary: The Oriental Institute, Baroda produced a critical edition of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (1960–1975), the text basis for the Princeton translation project.

date.note: Critical edition, Oriental Institute, Baroda (M. S. University).

sources.cite: Bhatt, G. H. & Shah, U. P. (eds.), The Vālmīki-Rāmāyaṇa (Baroda critical edition, 1960–1975).

proof.what: A collated archetype from manuscripts across recensions (N & S).
proof.establishes: The oldest recoverable common text of Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa.
proof.doesNotEstablish: Historicity of the narrative or an absolute date of first composition.

nodes.title: Rāma born in Ayodhyā
nodes.summary: Within the narrative, Rāma is born a prince of Ayodhyā, eldest son of King Daśaratha.

sources.cite: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla Kāṇḍa (Book 1).

image.alt: Rama breaking the bow of Shiva to win Sita — Raja Ravi Varma
image.credit: Raja Ravi Varma (1848–1906), ‘Rama breaking the bow’. Public domain (PD-Art).

nodes.title: Exile to the forest (14 years)
nodes.summary: On the eve of his coronation, Rāma is exiled for fourteen years; Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa accompany him.

sources.cite: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa (Book 2).

nodes.title: Sītā abducted by Rāvaṇa
nodes.summary: Rāvaṇa, king of Laṅkā, abducts Sītā; the search for her drives the rest of the epic.

sources.cite: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Araṇya Kāṇḍa (Book 3).

image.alt: Ravana abducting Sita, opposed by Jatayu — Raja Ravi Varma
image.credit: Raja Ravi Varma (1848–1906), ‘Jatayu Vadham’, oil on canvas, 1895. Public domain (PD-Art).

nodes.title: War in Laṅkā; return to Ayodhyā
nodes.summary: With the vānara army, Rāma crosses to Laṅkā, defeats Rāvaṇa, recovers Sītā, and returns to be crowned in Ayodhyā.

sources.cite: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Yuddha Kāṇḍa (Book 6).

nodes.title: The game of dice
nodes.summary: The Pāṇḍavas lose their kingdom, and Draupadī is staked, in a rigged game of dice — the wrong that sets up the war.

sources.cite: Mahābhārata, Sabhā Parva (Book 2).

nodes.title: Thirteen years of exile
nodes.summary: The Pāṇḍavas spend twelve years in forest exile and a thirteenth in disguise before returning to claim their share.

sources.cite: Mahābhārata, Vana & Virāṭa Parvas (Books 3–4).

image.alt: Draupadi as Sairandhri during the year in disguise — Raja Ravi Varma
image.credit: Raja Ravi Varma (1848–1906), ‘Sairandhri’ (Draupadi in disguise, Virāṭa Parva). Public domain (PD-Art).

nodes.title: The 18-day war at Kurukṣetra
nodes.summary: The war between Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas lasts eighteen days; the Bhagavad Gītā is spoken on its first day.

sources.cite: Mahābhārata, Bhīṣma–Śalya Parvas (Books 6–9); Bhagavad Gītā within Book 6.

nodes.title: Bhagavad Gītā becomes independently central
nodes.summary: Though a section of the Bhīṣma Parva, the Gītā came to be read, commented on, and transmitted as a standalone scripture — the most-commented Hindu text.

date.note: Later commentary tradition (Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja) makes it central in its own right.

sources.cite: Brockington, John (1998), The Sanskrit Epics. Leiden: Brill.

nodes.title: Kālidāsa, Raghuvaṃśa
nodes.summary: The classical poet Kālidāsa retells the Raghu dynasty (including Rāma's story) in courtly Sanskrit kāvya — an early literary reception of the Rāmāyaṇa.

date.note: Kālidāsa's dates are themselves debated; commonly placed in the Gupta era.

sources.cite: Kālidāsa, Raghuvaṃśa (ed. & trans. various).

nodes.title: Kambaṉ, Rāmāvatāram (Tamil)
nodes.summary: Kambaṉ's Tamil retelling (the Kamba Rāmāyaṇam) is a landmark of Tamil literature and a major regional reworking of the story.

date.note: Traditionally placed in the 12th century.

sources.cite: Kambaṉ, Rāmāvatāram (Kamba Rāmāyaṇam).

fidelity.note: Follows Vālmīki's arc closely but is an independent Tamil devotional reworking — a rough gauge, not a hard number.

nodes.title: Dāśaratha Jātaka (Buddhist, Pāli)
nodes.summary: The Buddhist retelling in the Pāli Canon (Jātaka 461) makes Rāma a bodhisattva; strikingly, Rāma and Sītā are SIBLINGS (not husband and wife), the exile is to the Himalayas, and there is no Laṅkā or Rāvaṇa. Some scholars argue it even predates Vālmīki. The seed of the epic's Buddhist, pan-Asian spread.

date.note: Dating and direction of influence (vs Vālmīki) are debated.

sources.cite: Dāśaratha Jātaka (no. 461), Khuddaka Nikāya, Pāli Canon.

fidelity.note: Same core figures but major departures (siblings, no Rāvaṇa/Laṅkā). Rough gauge.

nodes.title: Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (Java, Indonesia)
nodes.summary: The Old-Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa, composed in the Medang (Mataram) era, is the oldest surviving Ramayana in Southeast Asia. Its first half closely follows Vālmīki (via Bhaṭṭikāvya), then diverges — famously adding the clown-god Semar and sons. The story is carved at the 9th-c. Prambanan temple.

date.note: Medang/Mataram-era Old Javanese kakawin.

sources.cite: Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa (Old Javanese); cf. Prambanan reliefs, Java.

fidelity.note: First half close to Vālmīki, then local additions. Rough gauge.

nodes.title: China — via Buddhist texts & the Monkey King
nodes.summary: China received the Rāma story mainly through Buddhist literature (e.g. the Liudu ji jing / 'Collection of the Six Perfections', 3rd c. CE, includes a Rāma tale). Scholars widely note that Hanumān is an influence behind Sun Wukong, the Monkey King of the 16th-c. Journey to the West — a diffuse, transformed reception rather than a full retelling.

date.display: c. 3rd c. CE (Buddhist texts) → 16th c. (Sun Wukong)
date.note: Diffuse influence over a long span; the Sun Wukong link is a scholarly view, not a direct translation.

sources.cite: Liudu ji jing (六度集經, trans. Kang Senghui, 3rd c. CE); Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West (16th c.).

fidelity.note: Not a retelling — ethical fragments + a likely Hanumān→Sun Wukong influence. Rough gauge.

nodes.title: Japan — Hōbutsushū & the Bontenkoku tale
nodes.summary: Japan received the Rāma story through Buddhist collections — the Hōbutsushū (12th c.) and Sanbō-ekotoba (10th c.) carry versions, and the Bontenkoku tale localises it: Tamawaka (Rāma), a flute-player, rescues his wife Himegini (Sītā) from King Baramon (Rāvaṇa). A thoroughly localised, minor-key reception.

date.note: Sanbō-ekotoba c. 984 CE; Hōbutsushū 12th c.

sources.cite: Hōbutsushū (12th c.); Sanbō-ekotoba (c. 984 CE); Bontenkoku (otogi-zōshi tale).

fidelity.note: Heavily localised names & framing; only the core rescue survives. Rough gauge.

nodes.title: Reamker (Cambodia)
nodes.summary: Cambodia's Reamker (Rāmakerti) frames the story through Buddhist ethics — Rāma is Preah Ream, Sītā is Neang Seda. The earliest evidence is Angkor-period (9th–13th c.); the Angkor Wat murals carve Rāmāyaṇa scenes; literary/performance versions continue into the 16th–18th c.

date.note: Visual evidence from Angkor; later literary versions.

sources.cite: Reamker (Rāmakerti), Khmer; Angkor Wat reliefs (12th c.).

fidelity.note: Recognisable arc, Buddhist ethical reframing + Sītā's suffering expanded. Rough gauge.

nodes.title: Ramakien (Thailand)
nodes.summary: Thailand's Ramakien reframes Rāma as a KING (not an ascetic) — palace politics, war and court ritual dominate; forest renunciation shrinks. Versions circulate from the 14th-c. Ayutthaya period; the standard text was compiled by King Rama I (late 18th c.). Even the old capital 'Ayutthaya' echoes 'Ayodhyā'.

date.note: Rama I's standard version dated 1797 CE.

sources.cite: Ramakien (compiled King Rama I, 1797); Ayutthaya-period antecedents.

fidelity.note: Same skeleton, but kingship/warfare emphasised over renunciation. Rough gauge.

nodes.title: Phra Lak Phra Lam (Laos)
nodes.summary: The Lao national epic (Phra Lak = Lakṣmaṇa, Phra Lam = Rāma) arrived later than in Cambodia/Thailand, and lost its Hindu framing entirely — it is treated as a Jātaka, a former life of the Buddha. A vivid example of how far a story can travel and transform.

date.note: Later transmission; fully Buddhicised.

sources.cite: Phra Lak Phra Lam (Lao).

fidelity.note: Recognisable but fully Buddhicised, Hindu frame gone. Rough gauge.

nodes.title: Tulsīdās, Rāmcaritmānas (Awadhi)
nodes.summary: Tulsīdās's Awadhi devotional retelling (begun 1574 CE) is the most widely-recited Rāma text across North India and central to Rāmlīlā performance.

date.note: Composition begun at Ayodhyā, per the text's own colophon tradition.

sources.cite: Tulsīdās, Rāmcaritmānas (1574 CE onward).

nodes.title: Flying vehicles — the Vimāna, and its cousins elsewhere
nodes.summary: The Rāmāyaṇa's Puṣpaka Vimāna is a flying celestial chariot; the Mahābhārata has aerial craft too (Śālva's Saubha; Mātali flying Arjuna to Indra's heaven). Flying conveyances are a WIDE ancient literary motif — Greek sun/dragon chariots and Plato's winged chariot, Ezekiel's wheels and Elijah's chariot of fire, Etana borne aloft by an eagle in Mesopotamia. These are mythic/divine vehicles in stories, not evidence of ancient machines.

date.display: a shared ancient motif, c. 700 BCE – 500 CE
date.note: Comparative literary motif across cultures; dates are of the texts, not of any real craft.

sources.cite: Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (Puṣpaka Vimāna); Mahābhārata (Saubha; Mātali). For comparanda: Plato, Phaedrus; Book of Ezekiel; the Etana epic.
Wikipedia, 'Vimana' — overview of the motif and its sources (orientation).

proof.what: Flying-vehicle passages in the epics + parallel flying-conveyance motifs in Greek, Hebrew and Mesopotamian literature.
proof.establishes: That an aerial celestial vehicle is a genuine, canonical element of the epics — and a widely-shared ancient literary/mythic motif.
proof.doesNotEstablish: That any real ancient aircraft existed. The modern 'Vaimānika Śāstra' (dictated c. 1918–1923, published 1952/1973 — NOT ancient; no manuscript predates 1918) claims the vimānas were engineered planes; a 1974 Indian Institute of Science study (Mukunda et al.) found its designs unflyable. And the 'Inca / Nazca flying machine' idea is a modern fringe claim — the Inca (c. 1400–1533 CE) are late, had no writing, and describe no such craft.

nodes.title: Vimāna — the claimed design, engine & fuel (and the verdict)
nodes.summary: The EPICS give no engineering — vimānas are simply 'self-moving, mind-swift, sun-bright'. The specific design/engine/fuel 'specs' come ONLY from the Vaimānika Śāstra, a text dictated c. 1918–1923 (published 1952/1973), not an ancient source. It names four craft — Śakuna (bird-shaped), Rukma (gold, conical/pyramidal), Sundara (silver, rocket-like), Tripura (three-storeyed, air/water/space) — built of light heat-resistant alloys, driven by a 'mercury-vortex engine' (mercury + gyroscopic motion) with solar tubes, fuelled by quicksilver/'rasa'. A 1974 Indian Institute of Science study found the designs unflyable.

date.note: The design details are 20th-century, NOT from the ancient epics. Presented as what the claim says, with the scholarly verdict.

sources.cite: Josyer, G. R. (ed./trans.), Vaimānika Śāstra (attributed to Subbaraya Śāstry, dictated 1918–1923; Sanskrit+English 1973).

Mukunda, H. S., Deshpande, S. M., Nagendra, H. R., Prabhu, A. & Govindaraju, S. P. (1974), 'A Critical Study of the Work "Vymanika Shastra"', Scientific Opinion, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore.
Wikipedia, 'Vaimānika Shāstra' — dating + IISc study (orientation).

proof.what: The only source that gives vimāna 'engineering': the Vaimānika Śāstra's four craft (Śakuna/Rukma/Sundara/Tripura), light heat-resistant alloys, a mercury-vortex engine + solar tubes, quicksilver/rasa fuel.
proof.establishes: What the 20th-century claim actually specifies — and that a 1974 IISc engineering study reviewed it in detail.
proof.doesNotEstablish: That any of it flies or is ancient. The IISc study found no manuscript predates 1918, dated the text to ≥1904, and judged the craft 'poor concoctions' — aeronautically unfeasible, the propulsion resisting rather than assisting flight (only the Rukma duct-fan idea made partial sense). The epics themselves give NO such specs.

nodes.title: The Purāṇas absorb and retell
nodes.summary: The major Purāṇas (e.g. Viṣṇu, Bhāgavata) retell and frame both epics, embedding Rāma and Kṛṣṇa in the wider Vaiṣṇava avatāra scheme.

date.note: Purāṇic composition spans many centuries.

sources.cite: Rocher, Ludo (1986), The Purāṇas. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz.

nodes.title: Traditional authorship: Vālmīki & Vyāsa
nodes.summary: Tradition holds the Rāmāyaṇa was composed by the sage Vālmīki (the ādi-kavi, 'first poet') and the Mahābhārata by Vyāsa, who is also a character within it. This is the tradition's account, distinct from the philological picture of layered, multi-author growth.

date.note: Held within the tradition; not the scholarly view of composite authorship.

sources.cite: Rāmāyaṇa & Mahābhārata frame narratives (the texts' own accounts of their authorship).

nodes.title: Yuga chronology (Tretā / Dvāpara)
nodes.summary: Traditionally, the Rāmāyaṇa is placed in the Tretā Yuga and the Mahābhārata war at the junction of Dvāpara and Kali Yugas — commonly given as 3102 BCE for the start of Kali Yuga. These are traditional/astronomical reckonings, not academic datings.

date.note: The 3102 BCE figure derives from Purāṇic/siddhāntic reckoning (e.g. Āryabhaṭa's era). Presented as tradition.

sources.cite: Āryabhaṭīya (499 CE) and Purāṇic Yuga reckonings; discussed in Pingree, D., Jyotiḥśāstra (1981).

nodes.title: Archaeoastronomy dating claims
nodes.summary: Some authors retro-calculate planetary/eclipse references in the Mahābhārata to propose specific war dates (figures such as 3067 BCE and 5561 BCE circulate). These are contested and not accepted as mainstream academic dating; the described sky configurations are not uniquely datable.

date.note: Retro-calculation from textual sky references; method and premises are disputed by mainstream scholarship.

sources.cite: Popular archaeoastronomy proposals (e.g. B. N. Achar); critiqued in mainstream reviews — presented here as a claim, not consensus.

nodes.title: Hastināpura excavation & Painted Grey Ware
nodes.summary: B. B. Lal's Archaeological Survey of India excavation at Hastināpura (Meerut dist., UP) in 1950–52 identified a Painted Grey Ware (PGW) occupation dated to roughly 1100–600 BCE, and found evidence of a flood layer. Lal correlated PGW with the Mahābhārata milieu and the Purāṇic flood that moved the capital to Kauśāmbī. This correlation is DEBATED — later scholars have proposed other pottery/dates (OCP, ~2000 BCE) and critiqued the original argument.

date.note: PGW dating is solid; the PGW↔Mahābhārata correlation is contested. Recent dating at nearby sites complicates the picture.

sources.cite: Lal, B. B. (1954–55), 'Excavation at Hastināpura and other explorations in the Upper Gaṅgā and Sutlej basins 1950–52', Ancient India nos. 10–11, Bulletin of the ASI, pp. 5–151.
Wikipedia, 'Hastinapur' (overview + 2021–22 re-excavation) — for orientation, not as the primary source.

proof.what: A dated Painted Grey Ware cultural layer (and a flood deposit) at a site tradition names as the Kaurava capital.
proof.establishes: That an Iron-Age (PGW) settlement existed here c. 1100–600 BCE, and that a flood episode is recorded in the stratigraphy.
proof.doesNotEstablish: That the Mahābhārata war happened, nor that PGW people are the epic's characters. The PGW↔epic link is an interpretation, and a contested one.
proof.method: Stratigraphic excavation + Painted Grey Ware ceramic seriation, with a few scientifically-dated samples.

nodes.title: Sinauli cart/‘chariot’ burials
nodes.summary: ASI excavations at Sinauli (Baghpat dist., UP) uncovered copper-decorated solid-wheeled carts and rich burials dated to roughly 2000–1800 BCE. Some popular accounts call these 'war chariots' and link them to the Mahābhārata; specialists caution the solid-wheel carts are not the spoke-wheeled chariots the epic describes, and the link is speculative.

date.note: The dating of the burials is archaeological; the 'chariot' interpretation and any Mahābhārata link are disputed.

sources.cite: Sharma, S. K. et al., ASI Sinauli excavation reports (2018 season); summarised with cautions in academic reviews.

proof.what: Copper-fitted solid-wheeled carts and warrior burials of the early 2nd millennium BCE.
proof.establishes: A rich, possibly martial Bronze-Age burial culture in the western Gaṅgā–Yamunā doab.
proof.doesNotEstablish: That these are Mahābhārata 'chariots' or connected to the epic — the carts have solid, not spoked, wheels; the link is speculative.
proof.method: Stratigraphic excavation + typological dating; some radiocarbon context.

nodes.title: Ancient DNA — the peopling of South Asia
nodes.summary: The largest ancient-DNA study to date (Narasimhan et al. 2019, Science; 523 ancient genomes) reconstructs how South Asian populations formed: a gradient of Iranian-farmer-related, indigenous South-Asian (AASI), and — from ~4,000 years ago — Steppe pastoralist ancestry mixing over deep time. This is population history, on a far longer timescale than the epics as texts.

date.note: Genetic dating from ancient genomes; an evolving field with real uncertainty (ANI/ASI endpoints are inferred statistically).

sources.cite: Narasimhan, V. M. et al. (2019), 'The formation of human populations in South and Central Asia', Science 365, eaat7487.
Reich Lab open PDF of the above.

proof.what: Genome-wide data from 523 ancient individuals across South and Central Asia.
proof.establishes: A deep-time model of population movements and admixture (Iranian-farmer-related + AASI + Steppe) that shaped South Asian ancestry.
proof.doesNotEstablish: Anything about the Rāmāyaṇa or Mahābhārata as events, nor any identity between 'a genetic population' and 'the epic's characters or peoples'. Genetics is not the epic — and this is evolving science, not a verdict.
proof.method: Ancient DNA — genome-wide sequencing + population-genetics modelling (qpAdm, admixture graphs).

nodes.title: The Indus Valley (Rakhigarhi) genome
nodes.summary: The first genome of an individual from the Indus Valley Civilisation (Rakhigarhi, Haryana), reported by Shinde, Narasimhan et al. 2019 (Cell), showed a mix of Iranian-farmer-related and indigenous South-Asian ancestry — and, notably, no Steppe pastoralist ancestry. A single ancient genome, a data point in a still-forming picture.

date.note: One individual; conclusions are drawn cautiously from a single degraded ancient genome plus comparanda.

sources.cite: Shinde, V., Narasimhan, V. M. et al. (2019), 'An Ancient Harappan Genome Lacks Ancestry from Steppe Pastoralists or Iranian Farmers', Cell 179(3), 729–735.

proof.what: The first (and, at publication, only) sequenced genome from the Indus Valley Civilisation.
proof.establishes: That an IVC individual carried Iranian-farmer-related + indigenous South-Asian ancestry, without Steppe ancestry.
proof.doesNotEstablish: Any link to the epics or their characters; a single genome is a starting point, not a population, and certainly not a narrative.
proof.method: Ancient DNA from a single skeleton (Rakhigarhi) + comparison with the wider ancient-genome dataset.

nodes.title: Spitzer Manuscript reference
nodes.summary: The Spitzer Manuscript (a Sanskrit fragment from the Kizil caves, ~2nd–4th c. CE) contains what is often cited as one of the earliest surviving lists of the Mahābhārata's parvans (books).

date.note: Palm-leaf/birch fragment found near Kizil (Xinjiang).

sources.cite: Schlingloff, Dieter (1969), 'The Oldest Extant Parvan-List of the Mahābhārata', JAOS 89.

proof.what: An early manuscript fragment listing the epic's book-divisions.
proof.establishes: That a recognisable Mahābhārata parvan structure existed by roughly the early centuries CE.
proof.doesNotEstablish: The date of original composition, nor the events' historicity.
proof.method: Palaeography (script dating) + archaeological context of the Kizil find.

nodes.title: Early references & the epic's spread
nodes.summary: The Rāmāyaṇa story is attested early across Asia — e.g. reliefs and inscriptions in Southeast Asia and the Khmer world — showing wide diffusion well within the first millennium CE.

date.note: e.g. Rāmāyaṇa reliefs at Prambanan (Java, 9th c.) and Angkor (Cambodia).

sources.cite: Prambanan Rāmāyaṇa reliefs (Java, 9th c. CE); Angkor Wat reliefs (12th c. CE).

proof.what: Dated monumental reliefs depicting Rāmāyaṇa episodes outside India.
proof.establishes: That the narrative was widely known and depicted across Asia by the mid-first millennium CE.
proof.doesNotEstablish: A composition date for Vālmīki's text, nor historicity of events.
proof.method: Art-historical + architectural dating of the monuments (inscriptional & stylistic).
